prompt: Why is it called a *reverse* proxy?
hint: Whom does an office's proxy work for?

choices.text: It works for the server, where an ordinary proxy works for the client
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: It reverses the order of the headers
choices.why: Header order is not what the name is about.

choices.text: It sends the response before the request
choices.why: Nothing can answer before being asked.

choices.text: It connects from the server back to the client
choices.why: The client still connects to it; the proxy then connects onwards to the application.

prompt: After the first `proxy_pass`, the shop's `/api/echo` reported `peer` as `127.0.0.1` for every request. Why?
hint: Who opened the connection the shop received?

choices.why: Even a client across the world would show 127.0.0.1 now.
Right. The shop only ever sees the second connection.

choices.text: The shop hides addresses for privacy
choices.why: It printed exactly what its socket said.

choices.text: `X-Forwarded-For` replaced the address on the way
choices.why: No header was set yet; and a header never changes a socket's peer.

prompt: With `location /api/ { proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:8001/; }` (note the final slash), what path does the shop receive for `/api/books/3`?
hint: A path in proxy_pass replaces the matched part.

choices.why: That is what happens with no path in proxy_pass.
Right. `/api/` was replaced by `/`.
Nothing is added twice.
Only the matched prefix is replaced; the rest of the path stays.

prompt: Which variable gives the shop the name the browser asked for, without the port?
hint: `$http_host` keeps the port.

choices.why: That is the client's address.
That is http or https.
Right.
That is the list of addresses.

prompt: A client sent `X-Forwarded-For: 198.51.100.7` and the shop received `198.51.100.7, 127.0.0.1`. Which entry may the shop trust as the client's address?
hint: Who wrote each entry?

choices.text: The first, since it is the original client
choices.why: The client wrote it, so the client chose it.
One was written by your proxy and one by a stranger.

choices.text: The last one, added by Nginx
choices.why: Right. Trust what your own proxies added, nothing to its left.

choices.text: Neither: the header must always be ignored
choices.why: Your own proxy's entry is reliable; that is the point of the header.

prompt: The bookshop moves behind a cloud load balancer that sits in front of Nginx. In `X-Forwarded-For`, which entry now holds the real client's address?
hint: Count the proxies you run, from the right.

choices.why: The last is the load balancer, added by Nginx.
Right. One entry per trusted proxy, counted from the right.
The client can still write anything at the front.

choices.text: It is in `X-Real-IP` and nowhere else
choices.why: `X-Real-IP` set from `$remote_addr` would now be the load balancer.

prompt: Six requests through an upstream with no `zone` came back `shop1, shop1, shop1, shop1, shop2, shop1`. What explains it?
hint: How many workers are there?

choices.text: shop2 was slower than shop1 at the time
choices.why: Over a hundred requests they split fifty-fifty.

choices.text: Round robin picks a member at random
choices.why: It is a strict turn, kept per worker.

choices.text: Each worker keeps its own turn
choices.why: Right. `zone` shares one turn among them.

choices.text: keepalive pinned the connection to shop1
choices.why: Each curl was a new client connection; keepalive is towards the shop.

prompt: The directive that makes an upstream group's state shared by every Nginx worker is `___ shop 64k;`.
hint: Four letters.

prompt: Why does an upstream with `keepalive` also need `proxy_http_version 1.1` and `proxy_set_header Connection ""`?
hint: What does Nginx speak to the application by default?

choices.text: Without them Nginx speaks HTTP/1.0 and asks for each connection to be closed
choices.why: Right. Then nothing is left open to reuse.
Compression is gzip's business.
Neither says anything about encryption.

choices.text: They tell the shop to keep its own sessions
choices.why: Sessions are application state; this is about the connection.

prompt: With `weight=3` on shop1 and no weight on shop2, how many of 100 requests went to shop2?
hint: The default weight is 1.

prompt: While one four-second request ran on shop1, `least_conn` sent all four quick requests to shop2. What did it compare?
hint: Not requests sent: requests not yet finished.

choices.text: Requests in progress on each member
choices.why: Right. shop1 had one, shop2 none.

choices.text: The response time of each member's last request
choices.why: Nginx's open-source least_conn does not measure time.

choices.text: The CPU load of each machine
choices.why: Nginx cannot see the application's CPU.

choices.text: Each member's total requests since start-up
choices.why: That would be closer to round robin's view.

prompt: An application keeps each user's basket in its own memory, and runs as two copies. Which change removes the need for `hash $remote_addr` entirely?
hint: Where could both copies read the basket?

choices.why: That is the same affinity under another name.

choices.text: Adding a third copy of the application behind Nginx
choices.why: A third copy has a third, separate memory.

choices.text: A shared store for the baskets, like Redis
choices.why: Right. Then any copy can answer any request.
Connections to the application have nothing to do with where a basket is kept.

prompt: Match each situation to the upstream method that fits it.
hint: Lesson 2's table.

pairs.left: one member on a machine three times larger
some requests take seconds and some milliseconds
sessions live in each member's memory

prompt: With shop2 stopped, all six requests still answered 200. What did Nginx do with the first one sent to shop2?
hint: The error log says `Connection refused`, and the client saw 200.

choices.why: There is no cache yet.
Right. That is proxy_next_upstream.

choices.text: Waited for shop2 to come back
choices.why: It never came back during the test.
Nginx never starts the application; systemd does.

prompt: Both shops were started again, and the next request still got 502. Ten seconds later it got 200. Which setting explains the ten seconds?
hint: Its default is ten seconds.

choices.why: That one is sixty seconds by default and concerns slow answers.
That is a count of idle connections.
Right. A failed member is left alone that long.
That is a count of failures, not a duration.

prompt: What does `502 Bad Gateway` say about where the problem is?
hint: The gateway is the server in front.

choices.text: The client sent a malformed request
choices.why: That would be a 400.
A crashed Nginx answers nothing at all.
Right. Refused, closed or not HTTP.

choices.text: The application took too long to answer
choices.why: That is 504.

prompt: Why is an active health check not available in the Nginx this course installs, and what covers the gap?
hint: It is a product question, not a technical one.

choices.text: It is in the commercial NGINX Plus; systemd restarts the application and passive checks cover the seconds between
choices.why: Right.
HAProxy, Traefik and Caddy all do them.
There is no such module in open-source Nginx to remove.
Nothing to do with the address family.

prompt: `proxy_read_timeout 3s` and a five-second request: the client got 504 after six seconds, not three. Why?
hint: The log has two lines for one request.

choices.text: The timeout counts twice per request
choices.why: It counted once per member.

choices.text: It retried on the other member
choices.why: Right. proxy_next_upstream retries on a timeout.

choices.text: curl waited three more seconds on its own
choices.why: curl had no timeout of its own.
The reload had finished before the request.

prompt: Match each status to what Nginx is saying.
hint: Bad, unavailable, timeout.

pairs.right: the application did not answer properly
the application accepted and did not answer in time

right_distractors: the request body was too large

prompt: A `POST /api/orders` times out on shop1. Does Nginx send it to shop2?
hint: Would sending it twice be safe?

choices.text: Yes, exactly as it does for a GET request
choices.why: A GET is idempotent; a POST is not.
Not even once, by default.

choices.text: Only if keepalive is switched on
choices.why: Connection reuse does not change retry rules.
Right. An order sent twice is worse than one that failed.

prompt: A report legitimately takes forty seconds to build, and the API's `proxy_read_timeout` is 10 seconds. What should change?
hint: The rule has two halves.

choices.text: Raise the timeout for the whole site to 60 seconds
choices.why: Every other request then gets a minute to hang.

choices.text: A `location` of its own with a longer timeout
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Nothing; a 504 tells the user to wait
choices.why: A 504 is a failure, and the report is never seen.

choices.text: Add a second member to the upstream group
choices.why: The second member takes forty seconds as well, and gets the retry.

prompt: Why did `/covers/logo.svg` answer 404 even though `location /covers/` had the right `alias`?
hint: Regular expressions are tried after the prefix is found.

choices.text: The alias had no trailing slash at its end
choices.why: It had one; and the fix changed something else.
There was no exact location for that path.

choices.text: The `.svg` regex won over the prefix
choices.why: Right. `^~` stops the regex search.
With `^~` the same file was served.

prompt: Put Nginx's location selection in the order it happens.
hint: The exact match is the first thing tried.
items: An exact `=` match wins at once
The longest matching prefix is found and remembered
If that prefix has `^~`, it wins
Regular expressions are tried in file order
trap: Regexes are tried before the remembered prefix answers, which is what surprises people.

prompt: With `location /covers/ { alias /var/www/ipe/img/; }`, which file does `/covers/logo.svg` read?
hint: alias replaces the matched part.

choices.why: Right.

Paths are always under a root or an alias.

choices.text: Headers are stripped from errors for security

choices.why: Right. The forwarded headers are missing or not read.
